Yang Wang,‡a Yinlong Zhu,

CoS2–MoS2 nanoﬂakes decorated MoO2 (CoMoOS) hybrid submi-

cro-wires with rich active interfaces were synthesized via the

sulfuration of CoMoO4. They showed excellent activity while synergistically catalyzing the hydrogen evolultion reaction (HER) in

basic media by promoting both the water dissociation and hydro-

gen absorption steps. Thus, the CoMoOS catalysts only needed 123 mV to achieve 10 mA cm−2 with a small Tafel slope in alkaline

solutions, and required 1.68 V to obtain the same current density

when assembled into an alkaline electrolyser.

Hydrogen (H2), with the highest gravimetric energy density and zero carbon footprint, is widely considered as a promising energy carrier to fuel our society cleanly and sustainably. H2 produced by water splitting is highly desirable due to the large quantities of energy harvested without the emission of greenhouse gases and other undesirable side-products.1–3 Water splitting consists of two half reactions: anodic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and cathodic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) which is the actual process that generates H2.4,5 When OER and HER catalysts are assembled into an electrolyser, diﬀerent electrolytes including acidic, alkaline and neutral media can be used. Compared to a neutral electrolyser, acidic and alkaline ones are eﬃcient enough for commercial use. However, just a few non-noble metal compounds have been studied as OER electro-catalysts for acidic electrolysers,6,7

while most acidic electrolysers in acidic solutions still require

noble metal based catalysts such as IrO2 or RuO2 as OER electro-catalysts due to the instability of the earth-abundant transition metal compounds as OER electrocatalysts under a low pH condition.8,9 Therefore, the alkaline electrolyser will be more economical when assembled by non-noble metal based materials due to the cost-eﬀective and highly active earth– abundant OER electro-catalysts in basic media.10–17 However, HER kinetics are sluggish under alkaline solutions, almost two orders of magnitude slower than in acidic solutions.18–20 The sluggish kinetics in basic solutions impede the development of alkaline electrolysers based on non-noble metal electro-catalysts. Therefore, it is necessary to develop highly eﬀective HER catalysts in alkaline solutions based on cheap and earth-abundant elements.21–28

As a kind of non-noble metal catalysts, transition metal disulfides such as MoS2, NiS2, CoS2 and FeS2 always display good performance in acidic solutions.29–35 For example, MoS2 has emerged as a highly active noble metal-free HER catalyst in acidic solutions; however, its HER performance in alkaline solutions is inferior to that in acidic media, due to the sluggish water dissociation kinetics.36 In general, the HER process in alkaline media typically involves two steps: electron-coupled water dissociation to form Had (the Volmer step) and the concomitant conversion of Had into molecular H2 (the Heyrovsky or Tafel step).37–40 Therefore, promoting the water dissociation process is also crucial to an optimal HER catalyst operating in alkaline media besides tuning suitable hydrogen adsorption free energy. Recent studies have proven that oxides or hydroxides (e.g., NiO, TiO2, Mn3O4, NiTiO3, Ni(OH)2, Co(OH)2 and NiCo2O4) can eﬀectively facilitate water dissociation.41–47

Besides, MoO2 was also demonstrated to have a metallic property and reasonable HER activities.48 Therefore, various hybrid materials have been developed as eﬃcient HER catalysts in alkaline media owing to the synergistic eﬀect produced by the interfacial interaction between multiple components.49–52

Based on the above considerations, we postulated that ultrathin MoS2–CoS2 nanoflakes decorated MoO2 submicrowires could synergistically facilitate the HER process in alkaline

solutions, which followed the design criteria of eﬀective nonnoble metal HER catalysts in alkaline solutions: (1) appropriate hydrogen adsorption ability of metal disulfides (MoS2 and CoS2) and favourable water-dissociation (MoO2) during HER by introducing appropriate components; (2) exposing more active sites by nano-size-tuning the active components (nanoflakes) to obtain high electrochemical surface area (ECSA); (3) enhanced charge transfer during the electrochemical catalytic process (MoO2). The obtained MoS2–CoS2@MoO2 (CoMoOS) hybrid shows high HER performance with a small overpotential of 123 mV to achieve 10 mA cm−2 and a low Tafel slope of 86 mV dec−1 in the alkaline solution. The morphology of CoMoOS was first examined by scanning electron micron microscopy (SEM) (Fig. 1a), the diameter of CoMoOS wires is between 100 and 400 nm and the surface is much rougher than its CoMoO4 precursor (Fig. 1a, inset). This rough surface consists of nano-flakes, according to the low-magnification TEM image (Fig. 1b, inset), which can be further confirmed by the HR-TEM image (Fig. 1b) in which the lattice fringes with an interplanar spacing of 0.63 and 0.25 nm correspond to the (002) plane of MoS2 and the (210) plane of CoS2, respectively. The composition of CoMoOS was also determined by XRD patterns (Fig. 1c). The characteristic peak at 16.7 corresponds to the (002) plane in MoS2 (PDF No. 04-004-5723) which has a Molybdenite-2H phase structure. Another characteristic peak at 30.4 is ascribed to the (011) plane in MoO2 (PDF No. 04-007- 2356) with a Tugarinovite phase structure. The other obvious peaks at 32.5, 37.8, 42.4, 46.7, 54.5, 64.9, 68.2, 71.4 and 74.5 belong to the (111), (200), (210), (211), (220), (311), (222), (023) and (321) planes, respectively, in CoS2 (PDF No. 04-003-1962) of a Cattierite phase structure. Besides, the percentage (mass) of MoO2, MoS2 and CoS2 in CoMoOS were estimated to be 1.6%, 72.5% and 25.9% by XRD quantitative analysis – the Rietveld method (Table s1, ESI†). The E1g, E2g 1 and A1g modes belonging to MoS2 were also detected in CoMoOS as shown in the Raman spectra (Fig. s2, ESI†).

In order to identify the distributions of all elements in CoMoOS, STEM-EDS element mappings are shown in Fig. 1d, which show the uniform distribution of Co, Mo, S and O along the wire, demonstrating that the in situ generated CoS2, MoS2 and MoO2 are mixed at the nanoscale, providing many favourable interfaces. Qualitative evidence provided by XPS (Fig. s3, ESI†) confirmed that the surface of CoMoOS (top few nm) consisted mainly of the metal sulfides (CoS2 and MoS2) with a minor concentration of oxides, which may result from a slight surface oxidation of the sample in air.53,54

The optimal sulfuration condition was obtained by studying the influence of sulfuration temperature and duration, diﬀerent mass of sulfur as well as using a spacer boat during the sulfuration of CoMoO4 (Fig. s8†). When CoMoO4 underwent sulfuration at a temperature of 500 °C for 30 minutes by using 1.5 g of sulfur, the obtained CoMoOS showed the best HER performance among all the conditions studied. When a spacer boat between the boats containing sulfur and CoMoO4 was used, the performance was further improved by reducing 26 mV of the overpotential to obtain a current density of 10 mA cm−2. To better understand the function of the spacer boat, the CFD model (Fig. s9†) was applied to describe the eﬀect of the spacer boat on the flow of nitrogen as a carrier gas in the sulfuration process. The CFD calculation result shows that adding a spacer between the boats can lead to a more developed turbulent flow due to the developing reversed flow near to the boats’ edges. As a result, a better mixing of sulfur and CoMoO4 can be achieved at higher turbulence caused by the spacer boat. The electro-catalytic performance of CoMoOS was evaluated by the polarization curves from linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in 1.0 M KOH electrolyte using copper foam (CF) as the current collector. The LSV curves are obtained at a slow scan rate of 5 mV s−1 to minimize the capacitive current. All potential values presented in this work were iR-corrected (aiming to remove the ohmic potential drop) and referenced to the hydrogen electrode (RHE) unless indicated otherwise. For comparison, similar measurements are performed on CoMoOS, MoO2, MoS2, CoS2 and the physical mixture of MoO2/MoS2/CoS2. The morphology and XRD patterns of commercial MoO2 and synthesized MoS2 and CoS2 are displayed in Fig. s4.† From Fig. 2a, it is obvious that CoMoOS exhibits a very small onset potential of 65 mV and an low overpotential (η10) of 130 mV to achieve a current density of 10 mA cm−2 while the copper foam (CF) substrate has a negligible activity towards HER in 1.0 M KOH. However, CoMoO4 displays a large overpotential of 214 mV to achieve a current density of 10 mA cm−2. As for the single component of MoS2 and CoS2, their η10 are 302 mV and 273 mV, respectively, while the η10 of MoO2 is much more than 320 mV. When MoO2, MoS2 and CoS2 were physically mixed together (denoted as MoO2/MoS2/CoS2) according to the mass ratio detected by XRD, the overpotential to achieve 10 mA cm−2 is 258 mV which is lower than that of the single components but still much larger than that of CoMoOS, which demonstrates the favourable functions of each component as well as the synergistic eﬀects of the components in the nano-

hybrid. To get rid of the eﬀect from the porous substrate, glassy carbon (GC) was also used to test the performance of these catalysts (Fig. s5, ESI†) and CoMoOS also displayed the best performance among these catalysts. As an important parameter of electrolysis, the Tafel slope describes the over-potential needed to increase the current density by ten-fold, which reflects the kinetics of HER. Compared with CoMoO4 (133 mV dec−1), CoMoOS has a smaller Tafel slope of 86 mV dec−1 (Fig. 2b), demonstrating its fastest kinetics towards HER, while the Tafel slopes of MoO2, MoS2, CoS2 and the MoO2/MoS2/CoS2 physical mixture are 334, 120, 180 and 135 mV dec−1. Hence, CoMoOS hybrid possesses the fastest HER kinetics process among all the catalysts reported in this work. According to the mechanism of hydrogen evolution, the HER process consists of two principal steps in alkaline electrolytes. The initial discharge step is called the Volmer reaction (H2O + e−→Hads + OH−) with a high Tafel slope of 120 mV dec−1. Then, Heyrovsky reaction (the electrochemical desorption step): Hads + H2O + e−→H2 + OH−or Tafel reaction (the recombination step): Hads + Hads →H2 happens after the Volmer reaction with a relative lower Tafel slope of 40 and 30 mV dec−1, respectively. The Tafel slope of CoMoOS is 86 mV dec−1 which lies between 40 and 120 mV dec−1, suggesting that a Volmer–Heyrovsky mechanism might be responsible for the HER process in CoMoOS. The stability of CoMoOS for HER is also excellent with just 106 mV increase after electrolysis at −10 mA cm−2 for 40 h (Fig. 2c). The LSV recorded before and after the 40 h of testing at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1 are shown in Fig. 2d. Only a minimal loss in activity at a current density of 10 mA cm−2 is observed. Therefore, there is a very good agreement between the galvanostatic stability tests, reaﬃrming that CoMoOS is potentially a

very stable catalyst. Regarding the mass loading eﬀect, HER performance can be improved when the mass loading of CoMoOS is tripled from 0.8 to 2.4 mg cm−2. When the mass loading was further increased, the HER performance decreased due to the overloaded catalysts on the limited surface of the copper foam (Fig. 2d). The superior HER performance of CoMoOS compared to the CoMoO4 precursor and the single components as well as the MoO2/MoS2/CoS2 physical mixture might be due to the following three aspects: (1) Synergetic eﬀects between diﬀerent components of CoMoOS. Although MoS2 and CoS2 are favourable to hydrogen adsorption during HER, their performance in alkaline solutions is still limited by the sluggish water dissociation step which can be facilitated by transition metal oxides.36,46,55–57

Thus, introducing MoO2 can improve the HER performance of the whole hybrid by promoting the water dissociation during the Volmer step. Besides, the introduction of MoO2 with metallic properties will also improve the charge transfer of the hybrid according to the reports in the previous literature.58

Therefore, a similar mechanism is proposed here that MoO2 acts as the water dissociation facilitator while CoS2 and MoS2 together promote hydrogen absorption during the HER process (Fig. 3a). Besides, the uniform distribution of Co, Mo, O and S (Fig. 1d) indicates intimate interactions among CoS2, MoS2 and MoO2, which leads to strong electron interactions and enable the surface electronic state to reach a favourable hydrogen absorption free energy for the promotion of HER. (2) A one dimensional hierarchical structure with a high electrochemical surface area (ECSA) of CoMoOS. The hierarchical structure enables the hybrid with various sizes of channels and pores for mass transport (Fig. s1a and b, ESI†). For example, the macropores or channels originating from the interlacing of the one dimensional sub-microwires can facilitate mass (electrolyte or gas products) transfer. Besides, the meso-pores formed by the stacking of the CoS2 and MoS2 nanoflakes can provide high ECSA and expose plenty of active sites for HER. ECSA was calculated from the specific capacitance. Normally, the specific capacitance for 1 cm2 of a flat surface is around 20–60 μF cm−2 and the average value of 40 μF cm−2 is generally used for calculations. The specific capacitance (Fig. 3d) can be obtained from the geometric current density collected from the rectangular CV plots (Fig. 3c) at a certain potential of 0.15 V vs. RHE. The specific capacitance of CoMoOS is 46.3 mF cm−2 which is larger than that of CoMoO4 (2.7 mF cm−2), MoO2 (1.5 mF cm−2) and CoS2 (24.6 mF cm−2), due to the nanosize of the active CoS2 and MoS2 nanoflakes which can expose more active sites. Although the MoS2 and MoO2/MoS2/CoS2 mixture shows a higher specific capacitance than that of CoMoOS due to the nanosheet structure of MoS2 (Fig. s2b and e, ESI†) with a higher surface area, the intrinsic poor conductivity of MoS2 hinders the charger transfer which decreases the HER performance of both MoS2 (89.8 mF cm−2) and MoO2/MoS2/CoS2 mixture (60.4 mF cm−2). The high specific capacitance of CoMoOS demonstrates that there are a large amount of exposed active sites in CoMoOS for HER. The high ECSA might be derived from the meso-pores (typical plot for meso-pores in Fig. s1a, ESI†) stacked by MoS2 and CoS2 on the surface of MoO2. The diameter of the pore is around 20–150 nm (Fig. s1b, ESI†). In contrast, the smooth surface of CoMoO4 (Fig. 1b, inset) and bulk MoO2 (Fig. s4a and d, ESI†) enable them with very low ECSA, demonstrating the importance of the nano-design of the active components in the hybrid. (3) Low charge transfer resistance. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out to investigate the HER process of catalysts in this work (Fig. 3b). The EIS data of CoMoOS was fitted using the equivalent circuit model which showed two semi-circles (Fig s6, ESI†). The semicircle at high frequency reflected the contact resistance between the copper foam and CoMoOS, while the semicircle in the middle and low frequencies related to the charge transfer on the surface of the catalyst.62,63 Charge transfer resistance (Rct) is usually used to assess the kinetics of the electrochemical process on the surface of catalysts. The smaller the Rct reflects the faster the kinetics, thus leading to a larger current density. The results for the elements in the circuit are shown in Table s2.† The CoMoOS displays the smallest diameter of the semicircle shown in the electrochemical impedance diagram (Fig. 3b) which represents the smallest charge transfer resistance (∼2.1 ohm) during the HER process; in contrast, the

charge transfer resistance of CoMoO4, MoO2, MoS2 and CoS2 and the MoO2/MoS2/CoS2 mixture is 8.9, 104, 53, 42 and 21 ohm, respectively. The favourable charge transfer of CoMoOS is ascribed to its favourable nano-interfaces which boost the charge transfer. In addition to the high HER activity in alkaline solutions, CoMoOS also showed high OER performance (Fig. s7, ESI†) in alkaline media with a small overpotential of 260 mV to achieve 10 mA cm−2 and a low Tafel slope of 75.2 mV dec−1. To demonstrate the feasibility of using CoMoOS as both cathode and anode for overall water splitting (Fig. 4a), only 1.68 V is needed to achieve 10 mA cm−2 while the MoO2/MoS2/CoS2 mixture needs 1.74 V to reach 10 mA cm−2. The copper foam substrate shows negligible performance for water splitting. The potential of CoMoOS for water splitting is lower than other catalysts reported recently (Fig. 4c). The stability of CoMoOS for overall water splitting is excellent with just a 38 mV increase after 24 h electrolysis at a current density of 10 mA cm−2 (Fig. 4b). Gas bubbles were observed at both electrodes in Fig. 4d.

## Conclusions

Ultrathin CoS2–MoS2 nanoflakes decorated MoO2 microwires were successfully prepared via partial sulfuration. The obtained CoMoOS showed a high HER performance which is ascribed to synergistic eﬀects among MoO2, CoS2–MoS2, high ECSA (double-layer capacitance 46.3 mF cm−2) derived from its

The catalyst also shows a high OER performance and could be assembled into an alkaline electrolyser for water splitting with a low potential of 1.68 V in alkaline solutions. The synergistic hybridization of nano-flaked MoS2 and CoS2 with MoO2 provides insight into the design and fabrication of promising hierarchical structures for hydrogen evolution in alkaline media.
